note: Shared validation vectors for the #3963 (S4) abort sentinel. Evaluated against the real validators by modules/agent-factory/agent/src/control-abort-sentinel.test.ts (validateAbortSentinel) and modules/agent-factory/agent-worker-image/tests/test_abort_sentinel.py (validate_abort_sentinel). Both runtimes must agree on every vector, and the fixture exists because source-text constant matching could not catch the divergences that actually occurred: the constants matched exactly while Python honoured `version: true` (True == 1) and TypeScript rejected it, and later while TypeScript accepted `generation: 1.0` and Python did not. Four tables, because the contract has four separable parts: `vectors` (is this a well-formed sentinel for this run, which as of review finding 1 REQUIRES a gateway acceptance receipt and not a self-written `delivery` literal), `generation_binding_vectors` (what the env-supplied generation may be), `reason_vectors` (what operator text is derived from the signed body), and `byte_boundary_vectors` (the file ceiling, in bytes). Contains no credential: the signed bodies here are base64 of ordinary JSON, and no vector carries a real envelope — signature behaviour is covered by tests/test_abort_authorization.py with keys generated per run.
abort_receipt_note: The acceptance receipt every accepting document in `vectors` carries. It is NOT a real token and is signed by nothing: it has the three-part shape only so that it is a plausible value for the field, and no vector in this file is authorized. It replaced a top-level `accepted_delivery: "accepted"` literal, which was the subject of #3963 review finding 1 — the pod can write eight characters, so requiring them constrained only the honest writer. What both readers now pin here is the *shape* rule: the field is REQUIRED, must be a non-empty string, and is bounded by `max_envelope_length`. Whether the token actually verifies is a separate question, answered by the real gateway key in tests/test_abort_authorization.py; a document accepting in this table means only that it parsed as a sentinel bound to `binding`. Its length is deliberately even-parity with the rest of the base document so that `byte_boundary_vectors` can land on exactly `max_sentinel_bytes` with a whole number of 2-byte pad characters; without that the multibyte at-ceiling vector could not pin the bound as inclusive.
signed_body_note: The base64 body every accepting document in `vectors` carries, and the value both suites build their own valid documents from. It decodes to {"command_id":"cmd-0001","reason":"wrong branch"} — ordinary JSON, no credential. It is NOT signed: no vector in this file carries a real envelope, so nothing here is authorized, and a vector accepting means only that the document parsed as a sentinel bound to `binding`. The digest binding between these bytes and an envelope's `body_digest` claim is covered by tests/test_abort_authorization.py, which generates its keys per run.
envelope_note: The `envelope` field is the gateway's signed authorization for the abort. Both validators surface it without judging it — the signature is checked by whoever acts on the sentinel — so what has to agree across the runtimes is the *normalization*: which values become a token and which become exactly null, so that "no proof" is one state and not several shapes. `expect_envelope` pins that. Envelope vectors are ASCII only on purpose: Python bounds the field in UTF-8 bytes and TypeScript in UTF-16 code units, and a multi-byte vector would be pinning that difference rather than the rule. Note that an accepted vector here means only that the document PARSED — `abort_receipt` and `signed_body_base64` are required for that, but nothing in this table is authorized. The envelope and the receipt are deliberately normalized DIFFERENTLY: an unusable envelope becomes exactly null and the document still parses, whereas an unusable receipt refuses the document outright. That asymmetry is the point of #3963 review finding 1 — the envelope is a binding for the reason text, while the receipt is the acceptance proof itself, and a missing acceptance proof must never read as an accepted abort.

vectors.name: valid
vectors.note: the ordinary accepted case: version-exact and bound to this run and generation

vectors.name: valid_without_a_reason
vectors.note: an operator need not supply a reason; null must not become the string "null"

vectors.name: version_boolean_true
vectors.note: the divergence root found: isinstance(True, int) is True in Python, so this validated there and was rejected by TypeScript's strict !==. The schema version must be an actual integer.

vectors.name: generation_boolean_true
vectors.note: same bool/int hazard on the generation: JSON true must not read as generation 1

vectors.name: version_newer
vectors.note: exact match, not a minimum: a newer payload may narrow the abort's scope in a field this reader does not know to look at

vectors.name: version_older
vectors.note: both halves ship in one image, so a version mismatch means something is genuinely wrong

vectors.name: version_string
vectors.note: a stringly-typed version is not this schema

vectors.name: different_run
vectors.note: the failure this binding exists to prevent: honouring it would delete an unrelated live run's queue message

vectors.name: superseded_generation
vectors.note: generation is equality, not "at least": an abort aimed at an attempt that already ended must not finalize its replacement

vectors.name: future_generation
vectors.note: a generation this run never reached is not this run's abort

vectors.name: generation_string
vectors.note: inside the document the generation is a number; the decimal-string form is only accepted for the env-supplied binding

vectors.name: generation_fractional
vectors.note: a generation counts registrations; a fraction is not one

vectors.name: run_id_missing
vectors.note: an unbindable document cannot be validated, so it is not an abort

vectors.name: run_id_blank
vectors.note: blank is not a run identity

vectors.name: run_id_wrong_type
vectors.note: a numeric run id would compare unequal anyway, but the type check is the documented rule

vectors.name: command_id_missing
vectors.note: the command id is the evidence correlator; without it the abort cannot be traced to an accepted command

vectors.name: command_id_blank
vectors.note: blank is not a command id

vectors.name: command_id_wrong_type
vectors.note: required fields are type-checked rather than coerced

vectors.name: requested_at_missing
vectors.note: the request time is part of the evidence record

vectors.name: requested_at_blank
vectors.note: blank is not a timestamp

vectors.name: empty_object
vectors.note: no fields at all

vectors.name: not_an_object_list
vectors.note: JSON parsers happily return a list; field access on it would raise in the one place that must not raise

vectors.name: not_an_object_string
vectors.note: a bare string is not a sentinel, however suggestive its content

vectors.name: not_an_object_number
vectors.note: a bare number is not a sentinel

vectors.name: not_an_object_null
vectors.note: JSON null parses successfully and must still mean no abort

vectors.name: not_an_object_true
vectors.note: JSON true parses successfully and must still mean no abort

vectors.name: envelope_carried_through
vectors.note: the authorization is surfaced verbatim: it is a signature over exact bytes, so any normalization would invalidate it

vectors.name: envelope_absent_is_null
vectors.note: a well-formed sentinel with no proof still parses; it is refused at the authorization step, not here

vectors.name: envelope_empty_string_is_null
vectors.note: blank normalizes to null so 'no proof' is one unambiguous state the consumer tests once

vectors.name: envelope_non_string_is_null
vectors.note: a non-string envelope cannot be a token; it must not reach a verifier as some other shape

vectors.name: envelope_number_is_null
vectors.note: same rule for a JSON number, which both runtimes would otherwise coerce differently

vectors.name: envelope_list_is_null
vectors.note: String(['adpe1']) is 'adpe1' in JS but "['adpe1']" in Python, so coercion would make the runtimes disagree

vectors.name: envelope_boolean_true_is_null
vectors.note: a JSON true must not become a truthy token on either side

vectors.name: envelope_oversized_is_null
vectors.note: beyond the 8192-byte envelope ceiling both verifiers apply; an over-long value cannot be a real envelope

vectors.name: envelope_at_ceiling_is_kept
vectors.note: exactly at the ceiling is still accepted, pinning the boundary as inclusive on both sides

vectors.name: abort_receipt_missing
vectors.note: the vector that carries finding 1. A sentinel with a genuine envelope and no receipt is what a run produces when it asked to abort but the gateway never accepted one — and it is also exactly what a pod fabricates, since an envelope is obtainable from any earlier issuance. An envelope proves the gateway ISSUED an authorization; only the receipt proves it was accepted against this live run after durable intent was recorded. Refused, where the removed `delivery: "accepted"` literal would have honoured it.

vectors.name: legacy_delivery_literal_is_not_an_acceptance
vectors.note: the regression vector for #3963 review finding 1, pinned at the READER rather than at signature verification. `delivery: "accepted"` was the field this contract used to require, and it is eight characters any process in the pod can write — the agent holds a `Bash` tool. Both readers must now ignore it completely: a document carrying the old literal and no `abort_receipt` is refused, so the removed field cannot be reintroduced as a fallback for compatibility without failing here. Without this vector a reader that accepted the literal whenever the receipt was absent passed the whole suite, because the deeper signature check refused the document later — which made the reader's own rule untested and one edit away from being the only gate.

vectors.name: abort_receipt_blank
vectors.note: an empty receipt is no receipt. Refused rather than normalized to null the way `envelope` is, because the envelope is optional to the parse and this field is not: collapsing it would turn a missing proof into an accepted document.

vectors.name: abort_receipt_wrong_type
vectors.note: a non-string receipt. Both readers require `isinstance(str)`/`typeof === 'string'` before the length test, so neither stringifies an object into a pseudo-token.

vectors.name: abort_receipt_boolean_true
vectors.note: `True == 1` hazards do not apply to a string field, but a truthiness test would accept this. Both readers type-check before testing emptiness.

vectors.name: abort_receipt_oversized
vectors.note: one past `max_envelope_length`. Refused, NOT normalized to null: an oversized receipt is an unusable proof and the document must not parse without one. Python bounds UTF-8 bytes and TypeScript UTF-16 units, so this vector is ASCII to pin the rule rather than the difference.

vectors.name: abort_receipt_at_ceiling_is_kept
vectors.note: exactly at the ceiling is kept, pinning the bound as inclusive on both sides.

vectors.name: signed_body_missing
vectors.note: without the preimage the finalizer holds a signed `body_digest` and nothing to check it against — the exact structural gap that let a fabricated reason be attributed to a human. Required, not optional.

vectors.name: signed_body_blank
vectors.note: an empty string is not a body; it must not read as "no reason supplied".

vectors.name: signed_body_wrong_type
vectors.note: a number would stringify differently in each runtime before being hashed.

vectors.name: signed_body_oversized
vectors.note: one past the base64 ceiling for the listener's 16 KiB body cap. Bounded like every other field: these bytes are attacker-influenced input read during teardown.

vectors.name: signed_body_at_ceiling_is_accepted
vectors.note: exactly at the ceiling still parses, pinning the boundary as inclusive on both sides. Validation does not decode or verify these bytes — that is `verify_abort_authorization`'s job — so a body that is well-formed base64 of nothing meaningful is a *parse* success and an *authorization* failure.

vectors.name: version_integral_float
vectors.note: JavaScript has one number type, so `JSON.parse('{"version":1.0}').version === 1` is true and the TS validator accepts it; Python's `json` produces a float, which a bare `isinstance(..., int)` rejected. Two validators accepting different documents is the bug, in either direction — so both now define an integral number identically: integer-valued, however it was spelled.

vectors.name: generation_integral_float
vectors.note: the same rule on the field that actually binds the run. This is the dangerous half of the divergence: Python is the process that deletes the queue message, so it must not refuse a document the writer's own validator accepts.

vectors.name: generation_above_max_safe_integer
vectors.note: 2^53. Above it an IEEE double no longer represents consecutive integers, so two distinct generations compare equal in TypeScript while Python's arbitrary-precision int distinguishes them. Refused by both rather than clamped: silently mapping it to a different number is how a stale sentinel comes to match a live run.

vectors.name: generation_at_max_safe_integer
vectors.note: 2^53 - 1 is representable in both runtimes, so it is refused for the ordinary reason — it is not THIS run's generation 3 — and not by the safety bound. Pins that the ceiling is exclusive of the largest exact value rather than swallowing it.

generation_binding_vectors.name: trailing_garbage
generation_binding_vectors.note: root's second finding: Number.parseInt('1junk', 10) returns 1, binding the run to a generation the input never expressed, while Python's int() raises on the same bytes

generation_binding_vectors.name: pep515_underscores
generation_binding_vectors.note: Python's int('1_0') is 10 and JavaScript's Number('1_0') is NaN — divergence in the other direction, so both sides reject it explicitly

generation_binding_vectors.name: explicit_plus
generation_binding_vectors.note: int('+3') is 3 in Python; the shared rule is bare ASCII digits only

generation_binding_vectors.name: non_ascii_digits
generation_binding_vectors.note: int('٣') is 3 in Python and Python's \d matches it; the shared rule is ASCII digits only

reason_note: The operator's reason, derived from the signed request body rather than read from a field beside it. `signed_body_base64` is the exact bytes the gateway's `body_digest` claim covers, so text parsed out of them is text the operator actually submitted. Each vector gives the decoded body and the reason both runtimes must produce. `null` means "no verified reason", and a caller seeing it must say nothing about a reason rather than fall back to any other field — falling back is precisely what allowed fabricated text to be attributed to a human.

reason_vectors.name: absent_reason
reason_vectors.note: an operator need not supply one; absence must not become the string "null"

reason_vectors.name: blank_reason
reason_vectors.note: whitespace-only is no reason; `null` rather than "" so `if reason` and `if reason is not None` cannot disagree

reason_vectors.name: whitespace_collapsed
reason_vectors.note: the reason is interpolated into a GitHub comment, so newlines must not be able to forge its layout — even though these bytes are signed, a signature over hostile text is still hostile text

reason_vectors.name: non_string_reason
reason_vectors.note: str()/String() of an object would put "{'injected': True}" in front of an operator, and the two runtimes disagree about what it produces

reason_vectors.name: over_long_reason
reason_vectors.note: re-bounded on the way out even though it came from signed bytes: the signature proves the operator sent this text, not that its length suits a comment. The listener's own bound (1000) is looser than this one.

byte_boundary_note: MAX_SENTINEL_BYTES is a limit on encoded UTF-8 bytes, not on characters or UTF-16 code units. Python enforces it on a binary read before decoding; TypeScript measures Buffer.byteLength before JSON.parse. Each vector below states the padding to place in an unknown extra field and whether the resulting file must be read or refused. `multibyte` uses a 2-byte character so that a character-bounded read would accept roughly twice the intended size — the divergence these vectors exist to pin. The ceiling is derived (max_signed_body_length + max_envelope_length + 2048 slack), not a round number: it was a flat 8192 while the document must hold a 21852-character base64 signed body, so a control request the listener fully accepts produced a document the writer stored and the reader then refused on size — an abort reported to the operator as recorded and then finalized as a crash.

byte_boundary_vectors.name: ascii_at_ceiling
byte_boundary_vectors.note: exactly at the ceiling is read, pinning the bound as inclusive

byte_boundary_vectors.name: ascii_one_past_ceiling
byte_boundary_vectors.note: one byte over is refused without being parsed

byte_boundary_vectors.name: multibyte_at_ceiling
byte_boundary_vectors.note: a 2-byte character filling the document to exactly the ceiling. Still accepted, so the byte rule is not being enforced as a stricter character rule by accident.

byte_boundary_vectors.name: multibyte_one_past_ceiling
byte_boundary_vectors.note: the real defect: ~4100 characters is under any character-bounded read of 8192, so Python's text-mode read returned the whole document and validated it while the declared limit was bytes. Refused on both sides now.
